body.objective: Students will be able to analyze given circumstances.
successCriteria: I can find a character's given circumstances in a script
I can use the "magic if" to make choices
I can identify objectives and beats in a scene
body.hook: In the 1890s, Russian director Konstantin Stanislavski grew tired of actors who declaimed lines and struck poses. He asked a simple question: what if actors behaved as real people would in those exact circumstances? That question still shapes almost every film and TV performance you watch.

vocabulary.definition: An approach to acting that seeks truthful behaviour in imaginary circumstances.
The facts of a scene: who, where, when, what happened before and what is happening now.
Asking "What would I do if I were in this situation?"
What a character wants in a scene.
A section of a scene where one objective or tactic is played; a new beat starts when it changes.
The thoughts and feelings beneath the words.

study.title: The Detective's Script
study.question: How do actors use the script to find truthful choices?
study.passage:
Scene (original, for this lesson):
A kitchen, 11 p.m. MAYA (17) is at the table with a university acceptance letter. Her FATHER enters in his work uniform.
FATHER: You're still up.
MAYA: Couldn't sleep.
FATHER: Your mother said there was mail.
MAYA: Just flyers. (She slides the letter under a placemat.)
FATHER: The shop called again. They want me on Saturdays too.
MAYA: That's good, right? More hours.
FATHER: More hours. (Pause.) You should sleep.
MAYA: Dad? (He turns.) Nothing. Goodnight.
Part 1, Given circumstances (15 minutes): Answer the five W's for each character using only evidence in the script, then add inferences (marked "I think").
Part 2, Objectives and beats (15 minutes): Mark where each beat changes. Write an objective as an active verb for each beat ("to protect him," "to get her to talk").
Part 3, Magic if (5 minutes): Write what you would do if you were Maya in this exact situation.
Part 4, Rehearse (15 minutes): Play the scene twice: once on the lines only, once playing objectives and subtext. Compare.
study.source: Original scene written for this lesson; Stanislavski's concepts summarized from standard acting texts.

study.product: Perform the scene (or another short two-person scene) with a partner and submit a character analysis: given circumstances, beats, objectives and three lines of subtext.

examples.title: Given circumstances

examples.answer: Late at night: tired, private, tension of something unsaid
examples.explore: How would the scene change at noon?

examples.title: Subtext
examples.problem: What is the subtext of "Just flyers"?
examples.answer: "I'm not ready to tell you; I don't want to add to your worries"

examples.title: Beat change
examples.problem: Where does a new beat begin?
steps: Look for a change in tactic or topic
examples.answer: When the father mentions Saturday shifts; Maya shifts from hiding to supporting

examples.title: Active objective
examples.problem: Turn "Maya feels guilty" into an objective.
examples.answer: "To protect her father from more stress"
examples.explore: Why is this easier to act?

practice.q: Why write objectives as active verbs?
practice.a: Actions can be played; feelings cannot be played directly.

practice.q: What clue in the scene shows money is tight?
practice.a: The father's extra shifts and repeating "more hours."

practice.q: How do you find a beat change?
practice.a: Look for a shift in topic, tactic or objective.

practice.q: What's the difference between evidence and inference?
practice.a: Evidence is in the script; inference is what you conclude from it.

practice.q: Why did Stanislavski want truthful acting?
practice.a: He wanted believable behaviour instead of artificial declaiming.

practice.q: How does subtext make a scene more interesting?
practice.a: The audience senses tension between what is said and meant.

practice.q: What might the father's "You should sleep" mean?
practice.a: He may sense something is wrong but avoids the conversation.

practice.q: How does the magic if help an actor?
practice.a: It connects the character's situation to the actor's own imagination and truth.

practice.q: How could an actor show subtext without changing the words?
practice.a: Through pauses, eye contact, tone and actions.

items.answer: Answers vary, for example "I want to tell you but I can't."
Asking what I would do if I were in the character's situation.

items.q: Why should objectives be active verbs?
items.answer: They give the actor something to do on stage.

items.q: Identify one given circumstance from the scene and its evidence.
items.answer: For example, late night: "11 p.m."

items.q: Explain how Stanislavski's system leads to truthful acting.
items.answer: Actors study circumstances, pursue objectives and imagine themselves in the situation, so behaviour is believable.

items.q: Compare playing the scene with and without objectives.
items.answer: With objectives, actors have purpose, tension and subtext; without, it is flat.
